Objectives

  • Solve quadratic equations by factoring and the zero product property, including equations with a greatest common factor and the difference of two squares.
  • Solve quadratic equations by taking square roots and by using the quadratic formula from the GED formula sheet.
  • Find the vertex, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts, and y-intercept of a parabola from its equation or graph.
  • Compare linear and quadratic functions given as equations, tables, graphs, or word descriptions.
  • Review the whole course and build a personal plan for test day.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen with a coordinate grid from −10 to 10 on both axes
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson, Study Sheet, and the full-course review checklist (in the Post Lesson)
  • A copy of the GED formula sheet (students should know exactly where the quadratic formula sits on it)
  • Scratch paper and pencils; an on-screen or handheld scientific calculator for the quadratic formula portion
  • Optional: index cards for a “factor pairs” table and a large printed parabola for labeling

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick problems that connect earlier weeks' skills (factoring, evaluating, slope) to today.
Direct instruction20Solving by factoring (6 min), square roots and the quadratic formula (6 min), parabolas (5 min), comparing linear and quadratic functions (3 min).
Guided practice15Six problems in pairs or along with you; check that every equation is set equal to zero first.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Post these as students arrive. Each one is a skill from an earlier week that today's lesson depends on.

  1. Factor x2 + 5x + 6.
  2. Evaluate x2 − 3x when x = −2.
  3. What is √81?
  4. What is the slope of y = −4x + 7?
  5. If two numbers multiply to give 0, what must be true about them?

Answers: (1) (x + 2)(x + 3)   (2) (−2)2 − 3(−2) = 4 + 6 = 10   (3) 9   (4) −4   (5) At least one of them must be 0.

Spend the most time on problem 5. It is the whole idea behind solving by factoring, and students who say it in their own words now will remember why the right side of the equation has to be zero.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. Solving quadratic equations by factoring (about 6 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A quadratic equation has an x2 term as its highest power. Its standard form is ax2 + bx + c = 0, where a is not 0. The GED formula sheet shows this form.
  • Most quadratic equations have two solutions (also called roots or zeros). Train students to expect two answers.
  • Zero product property: if A × B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0. This only works with zero. If (x − 2)(x + 1) = 6, you cannot set each factor equal to 6.
  • Four steps: (1) move everything to one side so the other side is 0; (2) factor, using the Week 7 methods (GCF first, then trinomial or difference of squares); (3) set each factor equal to 0; (4) solve each small equation and check.

Worked Example 1 (factoring a trinomial). Solve x2 − 5x − 14 = 0.

The equation already equals 0. Find two numbers that multiply to −14 and add to −5.

Factor pairs of −14: (1, −14), (−1, 14), (2, −7), (−2, 7). Only 2 + (−7) = −5.

Factor: (x + 2)(x − 7) = 0

Set each factor equal to 0: x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2; x − 7 = 0 gives x = 7.

Check x = 7: 49 − 35 − 14 = 0. Check x = −2: 4 + 10 − 14 = 0.

Answer: x = 7 or x = −2

Worked Example 2 (moving terms and a GCF). Solve 3x2 = 12x.

Move every term to one side: 3x2 − 12x = 0

Factor out the GCF, 3x: 3x(x − 4) = 0

Set each factor equal to 0: 3x = 0 gives x = 0; x − 4 = 0 gives x = 4.

Check x = 4: 3(16) = 48 and 12(4) = 48. Check x = 0: 0 = 0.

Answer: x = 0 or x = 4

Point out the trap: a student who divides both sides by x gets only x = 4 and loses the solution x = 0. Never divide both sides of an equation by a variable.

2. Square roots and the quadratic formula (about 6 minutes)

Talking points:

  • When there is no x term, isolate x2 and take the square root of both sides. Always write ±: x2 = 49 means x = 7 or x = −7.
  • When a trinomial will not factor easily, use the quadratic formula, which is on the GED formula sheet: x = (−b ± √(b2 − 4ac)) / (2a).
  • Have students label a, b, and c, including their signs, before substituting. Put negative values in parentheses.
  • Compute the part under the radical (the discriminant, b2 − 4ac) first, then the square root, then the two answers. The whole numerator is divided by 2a.

Worked Example 3 (quadratic formula, exact answers). Solve 2x2 + 3x − 5 = 0.

a = 2, b = 3, c = −5

b2 − 4ac = 32 − 4(2)(−5) = 9 + 40 = 49, and √49 = 7

x = (−3 ± 7) / (2 × 2) = (−3 ± 7) / 4

x = (−3 + 7)/4 = 4/4 = 1   or   x = (−3 − 7)/4 = −10/4 = −5/2

Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0. Check x = −5/2: 2(25/4) + 3(−5/2) − 5 = 12.5 − 7.5 − 5 = 0.

Answer: x = 1 or x = −5/2 (−2.5)

Worked Example 4 (quadratic formula, rounded answers). Solve x2 − 4x − 3 = 0. Round to the nearest hundredth.

a = 1, b = −4, c = −3

b2 − 4ac = (−4)2 − 4(1)(−3) = 16 + 12 = 28

x = (−(−4) ± √28) / 2 = (4 ± √28) / 2

√28 ≈ 5.2915, so x ≈ (4 + 5.2915)/2 ≈ 4.65 or x ≈ (4 − 5.2915)/2 ≈ −0.65

Answer: x ≈ 4.65 or x ≈ −0.65

Stress that −b means “the opposite of b.” Because b is −4, −b is positive 4. And (−4)2 is 16, not −16.

3. Graphs of quadratic functions: parabolas (about 5 minutes)

Talking points:

  • The graph of y = ax2 + bx + c is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. If a is positive it opens up and has a lowest point (minimum). If a is negative it opens down and has a highest point (maximum).
  • The vertex is the turning point. Its x-coordinate is x = −b/(2a). Substitute that x into the equation to find the y-coordinate. The vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry.
  • The y-intercept is c (set x = 0). The x-intercepts are the solutions of ax2 + bx + c = 0 (set y = 0). Connect this to section 1: solving the equation and finding the x-intercepts are the same job.
  • The x-intercepts are always the same distance from the axis of symmetry, which gives a quick check.

Worked Example 5 (key features of a parabola). For y = x2 − 6x + 5, find the y-intercept, the x-intercepts, and the vertex.

y-intercept: x = 0 gives y = 5, so (0, 5).

x-intercepts: x2 − 6x + 5 = 0 factors as (x − 1)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 1 or x = 5. The points are (1, 0) and (5, 0).

Vertex: x = −b/(2a) = −(−6)/(2 × 1) = 6/2 = 3. Then y = 32 − 6(3) + 5 = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4. The vertex is (3, −4).

Check: 3 is exactly halfway between the x-intercepts 1 and 5. Because a = 1 is positive, the parabola opens up and −4 is its minimum value.

Worked Example 6 (a word problem). A ball is thrown upward from the ground. Its height in feet after t seconds is h = −16t2 + 64t. What is the greatest height of the ball, and when does it land?

Greatest height is at the vertex: t = −b/(2a) = −64/(2 × −16) = −64/−32 = 2 seconds.

h = −16(2)2 + 64(2) = −64 + 128 = 64 feet.

It lands when h = 0: −16t2 + 64t = 0, so −16t(t − 4) = 0, giving t = 0 (the moment it is thrown) or t = 4.

Answer: greatest height 64 feet; it lands after 4 seconds.

4. Comparing linear and quadratic functions (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A linear function changes by the same amount each time x goes up by 1 (constant rate of change, a straight-line graph). A quadratic function's changes themselves change by a constant amount (constant second differences, a parabola).
  • Model with y = 3x + 1 and y = x2 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: the linear outputs 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 go up by 3 each time; the quadratic outputs 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 go up by 1, 3, 5, 7, which increase by 2 each time.
  • A quadratic that opens up eventually grows faster than any linear function, even if it starts lower. GED questions often ask which function is greater at a given x, or which has the greater rate of change over an interval. Have students compute values rather than guess from the shape.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Students work in pairs. After each problem, have one pair explain its steps aloud.

  1. Solve x2 + 7x + 12 = 0.
  2. Solve x2 − 49 = 0.
  3. Solve 5x2 − 20x = 0.
  4. Solve x2 + 2x − 7 = 0 with the quadratic formula. Round to the nearest hundredth.
  5. For y = x2 + 2x − 3, find the vertex, the x-intercepts, and the y-intercept.
  6. Is the function in this table linear or quadratic? x: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; y: 1, 3, 9, 19, 33

Answers:

(1) (x + 3)(x + 4) = 0, so x = −3 or x = −4.

(2) x2 = 49, so x = 7 or x = −7 (or factor: (x + 7)(x − 7) = 0).

(3) 5x(x − 4) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 4.

(4) a = 1, b = 2, c = −7; b2 − 4ac = 4 + 28 = 32; x = (−2 ± √32)/2; √32 ≈ 5.657; x ≈ 1.83 or x ≈ −3.83.

(5) Vertex: x = −2/2 = −1, y = 1 − 2 − 3 = −4, so (−1, −4). x-intercepts: (x + 3)(x − 1) = 0, so (−3, 0) and (1, 0). y-intercept: (0, −3).

(6) First differences: 2, 6, 10, 14. Second differences: 4, 4, 4. The second differences are constant, so the function is quadratic.

Checks for Understanding

  • Ask: “Why must one side be 0 before we factor?” Expected: The zero product property only works when the product is 0.
  • Ask: “How many solutions does x2 = 36 have?” Expected: Two: 6 and −6.
  • Ask: “In 3x2 − x − 7 = 0, what are a, b, and c?” Expected: a = 3, b = −1, c = −7.
  • Ask: “Does y = −2x2 + 3 open up or down? Does it have a maximum or a minimum?” Expected: Down, so it has a maximum, at (0, 3).
  • Ask: “A table's y-values go 5, 8, 11, 14. Linear or quadratic?” Expected: Linear, because it goes up by 3 every time.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

  • Not setting the equation equal to 0. Students write x(x + 3) = 10 and conclude x = 10 or x = 7. Correct by having them rewrite as x2 + 3x − 10 = 0 first, then factor: (x + 5)(x − 2) = 0.
  • Forgetting the negative square root. x2 = 25 has two answers, 5 and −5. Have students write ± every time.
  • Sign errors in the quadratic formula. When b is negative, −b is positive and b2 is positive. Require parentheses around every substituted value.
  • Dividing only part of the numerator by 2a. In (4 ± √28)/2, both the 4 and the square root are divided by 2. Have students compute the full numerator first.
  • Mixing up the intercepts. x-intercepts have y = 0 and are written (x, 0); the y-intercept has x = 0 and is written (0, y).
  • Dividing both sides by x. This loses the solution x = 0. Factor out x instead.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a factor-pair table to fill in before factoring. Start with equations where a = 1 and the solutions are positive. Provide a formula card with blank boxes for a, b, and c and for each step of the quadratic formula. Let students check solutions by substituting before they move on, so they get immediate feedback.

Stretch: Introduce the discriminant as a predictor: if b2 − 4ac is positive there are two real solutions, if it is zero there is one, and if it is negative there are none (the parabola does not touch the x-axis). Ask students to write a quadratic equation whose solutions are 3 and −5 (answer: (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0, or x2 + 2x − 15 = 0), and to explain why the vertex of y = (x − 2)2 + 1 is (2, 1).

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Formats: multiple choice (“What are the solutions of …?”), fill-in-the-blank (“What is the positive solution?”), drag-and-drop (placing factors or steps in order), drop-down menus inside a worked solution, and hotspot items where students click the vertex or an intercept on a grid.
  • Typical wording: “Which values of x satisfy the equation?”, “What is the vertex of the graph?”, “At what time does the object hit the ground?”, “Which function has the greater value when x = 5?”, “The length of a rectangle is 3 feet more than its width…”
  • Formula sheet: the standard form of a quadratic equation and the quadratic formula are on the sheet. The vertex formula x = −b/(2a) is not, so students must memorize it.
  • Calculator: the quadratic formula items usually appear in the calculator part of the test. Show students how to compute the square root and to store or rewrite it before adding and subtracting.

Teacher note: running the final review. This is the last week of the course. Walk students through the full-course review checklist in the Post Lesson during the wrap-up. Ask each student to mark every skill as “solid,” “shaky,” or “not yet,” then use their scores from earlier Practice GEDs to pick their top three review targets. The weekly practice items deliberately mix quadratics with percents, geometry, lines, and statistics so you can spot which earlier skills have faded.
student:
Welcome to Week 10

This is the final week of the course. You will learn the last big algebra topic on the GED math test, quadratics, and then put the whole course together. Quadratics use skills you already have: factoring (Week 7), solving equations (Week 8), and graphing (Week 9). Take each section one step at a time and write every step on paper.

1. What Is a Quadratic Equation?

A quadratic equation has x2 as its highest power. Its standard form is

ax2 + bx + c = 0   (a is not 0)

For example, in 2x2 − 7x + 3 = 0, a = 2, b = −7, and c = 3. Notice that the sign belongs to the number. Most quadratic equations have two solutions, so expect two answers.

2. Solving by Factoring

The key fact is the zero product property: if two numbers multiply to 0, at least one of them must be 0.

  1. Get 0 on one side of the equation.
  2. Factor the other side.
  3. Set each factor equal to 0.
  4. Solve each small equation. Check by substituting.

Example 1. Solve x2 + 2x − 15 = 0.

Find two numbers that multiply to −15 and add to 2: 5 and −3.

(x + 5)(x − 3) = 0

x + 5 = 0 gives x = −5.   x − 3 = 0 gives x = 3.

Check x = 3: 9 + 6 − 15 = 0. Check x = −5: 25 − 10 − 15 = 0.

Answer: x = −5 or x = 3

Watch out: The equation must equal 0 before you factor. If you see x2 + 2x = 15, subtract 15 from both sides first.

3. Solving by Square Roots

If there is no x term, get x2 alone and take the square root of both sides. Remember that a positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.

Example 2. Solve 3x2 = 75.

Divide both sides by 3: x2 = 25

Take the square root: x = 5 or x = −5 (written x = ±5)

Check: 3(25) = 75 and 3(−5)2 = 3(25) = 75.

4. The Quadratic Formula

Some quadratics are hard or impossible to factor. The quadratic formula always works, and it is printed on the GED formula sheet:

x = (−b ± √(b2 − 4ac)) / (2a)

Step by step: write down a, b, and c with their signs; compute b2 − 4ac; take its square root; then find the “plus” answer and the “minus” answer. Divide the whole top by 2a.

Example 3. Solve x2 + 6x + 2 = 0. Round to the nearest hundredth.

a = 1, b = 6, c = 2

b2 − 4ac = 36 − 4(1)(2) = 36 − 8 = 28

x = (−6 ± √28) / 2, and √28 ≈ 5.2915

x ≈ (−6 + 5.2915)/2 ≈ −0.35   or   x ≈ (−6 − 5.2915)/2 ≈ −5.65

Answer: x ≈ −0.35 or x ≈ −5.65

Tip: Put negative numbers in parentheses when you substitute. If b = −4, then b2 = (−4)2 = 16, and −b = 4.

5. Graphs of Quadratics: Parabolas

The graph of y = ax2 + bx + c is a U-shaped curve called a parabola.

  • If a is positive, it opens up and has a lowest point (minimum).
  • If a is negative, it opens down and has a highest point (maximum).
  • The vertex is the turning point. Its x-coordinate is x = −b/(2a). Substitute that value to get the y-coordinate. This formula is not on the formula sheet, so memorize it.
  • The y-intercept is c, the point (0, c).
  • The x-intercepts are the solutions of ax2 + bx + c = 0. They are points where y = 0.

Example 4. For y = −x2 + 4x + 5, find the vertex and the intercepts.

a = −1, so the parabola opens down.

Vertex: x = −4/(2 × −1) = −4/−2 = 2. Then y = −(2)2 + 4(2) + 5 = −4 + 8 + 5 = 9. The vertex is (2, 9), the maximum point.

y-intercept: (0, 5)

x-intercepts: −x2 + 4x + 5 = 0. Multiply every term by −1: x2 − 4x − 5 = 0, so (x − 5)(x + 1) = 0. The points are (5, 0) and (−1, 0).

6. Linear or Quadratic?

Look at how the outputs change when x goes up by 1.

x01234
Linear: y = 3x + 11471013
Quadratic: y = x2014916
  • The linear outputs always go up by 3: the same change every time. Its graph is a straight line.
  • The quadratic outputs go up by 1, 3, 5, 7. Those changes grow by 2 each time. Its graph is a parabola.

Notice that y = x2 starts lower, but by x = 4 it has passed the line. An upward parabola eventually beats any line. When a question asks which function is greater, substitute the x-value into both and compare.

Try It

1. Solve x2 − 9x + 20 = 0.

Show answer

Numbers that multiply to 20 and add to −9: −4 and −5. (x − 4)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 4 or x = 5.

2. Solve x2 − 64 = 0.

Show answer

x2 = 64, so x = 8 or x = −8.

3. Solve 2x2 − 7x + 3 = 0 with the quadratic formula.

Show answer

a = 2, b = −7, c = 3. b2 − 4ac = 49 − 24 = 25, and √25 = 5. x = (7 ± 5)/4, so x = 12/4 = 3 or x = 2/4 = 1/2.

4. Find the vertex of y = x2 + 8x + 10.

Show answer

x = −8/(2 × 1) = −4. y = 16 − 32 + 10 = −6. The vertex is (−4, −6).

5. A table has x-values 0, 1, 2, 3 and y-values 2, 5, 10, 17. Is the function linear or quadratic?

Show answer

The changes are 3, 5, 7. They are not the same, but they grow by 2 each time, so the function is quadratic.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • Standard form of a quadratic equation: ax2 + bx + c = 0. Expect two solutions.
  • To solve by factoring, get 0 on one side, factor, set each factor equal to 0, and solve.
  • If there is no x term, isolate x2 and take ± the square root.
  • The quadratic formula, x = (−b ± √(b2 − 4ac))/(2a), works for every quadratic and is on the formula sheet.
  • A parabola opens up when a > 0 and down when a < 0. Vertex: x = −b/(2a). y-intercept: c. x-intercepts: the solutions when y = 0.
  • Linear functions change by the same amount each step; quadratic functions do not, but their changes grow at a steady rate.

Exit Ticket

1. Solve x2 − 3x − 10 = 0.

Show answer

(x − 5)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −2.

2. Solve 4x2 = 36.

Show answer

x2 = 9, so x = 3 or x = −3.

3. Find the vertex of y = x2 − 4x + 1.

Show answer

x = 4/2 = 2; y = 4 − 8 + 1 = −3. Vertex (2, −3).

4. What is the y-intercept of y = 2x2 − 5x + 7?

Show answer

Set x = 0: y = 7. The y-intercept is (0, 7).

5. The y-values of a table are 7, 11, 15, 19 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Linear or quadratic?

Show answer

Linear. The values go up by 4 every time.

Reflection

  • Which method for solving quadratics (factoring, square roots, or the formula) do you trust most? When will you use each one?
  • Looking back over all ten weeks, which topic improved the most? Which one still needs work?
  • What is one habit (checking signs, writing every step, estimating) that you will use on every question on test day?

Test-Day Strategy for the Math Test

  • Pace yourself. You have 115 minutes for 46 questions, about 2.5 minutes each. If a question takes more than 3 minutes, flag it, make your best guess, and come back.
  • Part 1 has no calculator. The first five questions must be done by hand, and you cannot return to them after you move on to Part 2. Work them carefully.
  • Use the formula sheet and the calculator in Part 2, but estimate first so you notice a mistyped number.
  • Read the last sentence first. Know what the question asks (the width or the length? the time or the height?) before you start computing.
  • Plug answers back in. For equation questions, substituting an answer choice is often faster than solving and is a built-in check.
  • Answer every question. Wrong answers do not cost extra points, so never leave a blank.

notes:
Week 10 Study Sheet: Quadratics and Final Review

Solving Quadratics

Standard form: ax2 + bx + c = 0

  1. Factoring: get 0 on one side, factor, set each factor = 0. x2 − 5x − 14 = 0 → (x + 2)(x − 7) = 0 → x = −2, 7
  2. Square roots: no x term. 3x2 = 75 → x2 = 25 → x = ±5
  3. Quadratic formula (on formula sheet): x = (−b ± √(b2 − 4ac)) / (2a)

Factor patterns: GCF first; a2 − b2 = (a + b)(a − b).

Parabolas: y = ax2 + bx + c

  • a > 0: opens up (minimum). a < 0: opens down (maximum).
  • Vertex: x = −b/(2a), then substitute for y. Not on the formula sheet.
  • y-intercept: (0, c)
  • x-intercepts: solve ax2 + bx + c = 0; points (x, 0)
  • Axis of symmetry: the vertical line through the vertex, halfway between the x-intercepts.

Linear vs. Quadratic

LinearQuadratic
Equationy = mx + by = ax2 + bx + c
GraphStraight lineParabola
Table patternSame change each stepChanges grow by the same amount
Example1, 4, 7, 10 (+3 each)0, 1, 4, 9 (+1, +3, +5)

Memorize (not on the formula sheet)

  • Vertex: x = −b/(2a)
  • Percent change = change ÷ original
  • Mode (most frequent value); range = max − min
  • Probability = favorable ÷ total
  • Exponent rules and factoring patterns

On the formula sheet

  • Area and perimeter of squares, rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapezoids; circle area and circumference
  • Volume and surface area of solids
  • Mean and median (definitions)
  • Slope, slope-intercept, point-slope
  • Quadratic formula, Pythagorean theorem
  • Simple interest, distance, total cost

Top mistakes: not setting the equation to 0; forgetting the negative root; sign errors with −b and b2; dividing only part of the top by 2a; mixing up x- and y-intercepts; dividing both sides by x.

items.prompt:
What are the solutions of the equation below?

(x − 3)(x + 8) = 0
items.hint: Set each factor equal to 0 and solve each small equation.
items.explain:
By the zero product property, one of the factors must equal 0.

x − 3 = 0, so x = 3

x + 8 = 0, so x = −8

The solutions are x = 3 and x = −8. Check: (3 − 3)(3 + 8) = 0(11) = 0 and (−8 − 3)(−8 + 8) = (−11)(0) = 0.

The choice x = −3 and x = 8 comes from copying the numbers in the factors without solving. The solution always has the opposite sign of the number in the factor.

items.prompt: A family's monthly electric bill rose from $240 in April to $282 in July. What was the percent increase?
items.hint: Percent change = amount of change ÷ original amount. The original amount is the April bill.
items.explain:
Amount of change: $282 − $240 = $42

Divide by the original (April) amount: 42 ÷ 240 = 0.175

Change to a percent: 0.175 × 100 = 17.5%

14.9% comes from dividing by the new amount (42 ÷ 282 ≈ 0.149). Always divide by the original value. 42% treats the dollar change as a percent.

items.prompt: A circular rug has an area of 50.24 square feet. Using 3.14 for π, what is the radius of the rug, in feet?
items.hint: Use A = πr<sup>2</sup>. Divide by 3.14 to get r<sup>2</sup> alone, then take the square root.
items.explain:
Area of a circle: A = πr2

50.24 = 3.14 × r2

Divide both sides by 3.14: r2 = 50.24 ÷ 3.14 = 16

Take the square root: r = 4 (a radius cannot be negative, so −4 is rejected)

The radius is 4 feet. A common mistake is to stop at 16, which is r2, not r.

items.prompt:
What are the x-intercepts of the graph of the function below?

y = x2 − 2x − 8
items.hint: x-intercepts are where y = 0. Set x<sup>2</sup> − 2x − 8 equal to 0 and factor.
items.explain:
At an x-intercept, y = 0: x2 − 2x − 8 = 0

Find two numbers that multiply to −8 and add to −2: −4 and 2.

(x − 4)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 4 or x = −2

The x-intercepts are (4, 0) and (−2, 0).

(−4, 0) and (2, 0) is a sign error. (0, 4) and (0, −2) puts the values in the y-position; x-intercepts always have y = 0. (0, −8) is the y-intercept.

items.prompt: A line passes through the points (−2, 5) and (4, −7). Which equation represents the line?
items.hint: Find the slope with (y<sub>2</sub> − y<sub>1</sub>)/(x<sub>2</sub> − x<sub>1</sub>). Then substitute one point into y = mx + b to find b.
items.explain:
Slope: m = (−7 − 5) / (4 − (−2)) = −12 / 6 = −2

Substitute the point (−2, 5) into y = −2x + b:

5 = −2(−2) + b

5 = 4 + b, so b = 1

The equation is y = −2x + 1. Check with (4, −7): −2(4) + 1 = −8 + 1 = −7.

y = −2x + 9 comes from treating −2(−2) as −4. y = −½x + 4 comes from dividing the x-change by the y-change.

items.prompt:
A student solves the equation x2 − 2x − 24 = 0 by factoring. Choose the correct option for each step.

Step 1 (factor): {{0}} = 0

Step 2 (solve): {{1}}
items.hint: You need two numbers that multiply to −24 and add to −2.
items.explain:
Step 1: Two numbers with a product of −24 and a sum of −2 are −6 and 4, so the expression factors as (x − 6)(x + 4).

Check by multiplying: x2 + 4x − 6x − 24 = x2 − 2x − 24.

(x + 6)(x − 4) = x2 + 2x − 24 has the wrong middle sign. (x − 8)(x + 3) = x2 − 5x − 24 and (x − 12)(x + 2) = x2 − 10x − 24 have the wrong middle term.

Step 2: x − 6 = 0 gives x = 6; x + 4 = 0 gives x = −4. So x = 6 or x = −4.

Check x = −4: 16 + 8 − 24 = 0.

items.prompt: The length of a rectangular garden is 3 feet more than its width. The area of the garden is 70 square feet. What is the width of the garden?
items.hint: Let w be the width, so the length is w + 3. Area = length × width. Set up the equation, get 0 on one side, and factor.
items.explain:
Let the width be w. Then the length is w + 3.

Area: w(w + 3) = 70

Distribute: w2 + 3w = 70

Subtract 70: w2 + 3w − 70 = 0

Two numbers that multiply to −70 and add to 3: 10 and −7.

(w + 10)(w − 7) = 0, so w = −10 or w = 7

A width cannot be negative, so the width is 7 feet (and the length is 10 feet). Check: 7 × 10 = 70.

10 feet is the length, not the width. 8.4 feet is √70, which would be the side of a square, not this rectangle.

items.prompt:
A worker recorded the number of customers she served on each of six days:

12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 28

Which statements about the data are true? Select two answers.
items.hint: Mean = sum ÷ number of values. With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values.
items.explain:
Mean: 12 + 15 + 15 + 18 + 20 + 28 = 108, and 108 ÷ 6 = 18. True.

Median: the two middle values are 15 and 18, so the median is (15 + 18) ÷ 2 = 16.5. True.

Mode: 15 appears twice, so the mode is 15, not 20.

Range: 28 − 12 = 16, not 13.

A median of 15 comes from using only one middle value. A mean of 21.6 comes from dividing 108 by 5 instead of 6.

The true statements are the mean is 18 and the median is 16.5.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x2 + 4x + 1 is a parabola. Click the point on the grid that is the vertex of the parabola.
items.hint: The x-coordinate of the vertex is x = −b/(2a). Substitute it into the equation to find y.
items.explain:
a = 1 and b = 4.

x = −b/(2a) = −4/(2 × 1) = −2

y = (−2)2 + 4(−2) + 1 = 4 − 8 + 1 = −3

The vertex is (−2, −3). Because a is positive, it is the lowest point of the parabola.

A common mistake is to drop the negative sign in −b/(2a) and click (2, −3). But when x = 2, y = 4 + 8 + 1 = 13, so (2, −3) is not even on the graph.

items.prompt:
What are the solutions of the equation below, rounded to the nearest hundredth?

3x2 − 2x − 4 = 0
items.hint: Use the quadratic formula with a = 3, b = −2, and c = −4. Remember that −b is positive 2.
items.explain:
a = 3, b = −2, c = −4

b2 − 4ac = (−2)2 − 4(3)(−4) = 4 + 48 = 52

√52 ≈ 7.2111

x = (−(−2) ± 7.2111) / (2 × 3) = (2 ± 7.2111) / 6

x ≈ 9.2111 / 6 ≈ 1.535, which rounds to 1.54

x ≈ −5.2111 / 6 ≈ −0.869, which rounds to −0.87

The solutions are x ≈ 1.54 and x ≈ −0.87.

0.87 and −1.54 come from using −2 instead of +2 for −b. 3.07 and −1.74 come from dividing by a (3) instead of 2a (6). 1.22 and −0.55 come from computing 4ac as 24 instead of 48.

items.prompt:
A ball is tossed upward from the edge of a platform 160 feet above the ground. Its height h, in feet, after t seconds is given by

h = −16t2 + 48t + 160

How many seconds after it is tossed does the ball hit the ground?
items.hint: The ball hits the ground when h = 0. Divide every term by −16 before factoring.
items.explain:
The ball hits the ground when h = 0:

−16t2 + 48t + 160 = 0

Divide every term by −16: t2 − 3t − 10 = 0

Factor: (t − 5)(t + 2) = 0, so t = 5 or t = −2

Time cannot be negative, so the ball hits the ground after 5 seconds.

Check: −16(25) + 48(5) + 160 = −400 + 240 + 160 = 0.

A common mistake is to find the time of the greatest height instead: t = −48/(2 × −16) = 1.5 seconds. That is when the ball is highest, not when it lands.

items.prompt:
Function f is linear. Some of its values are shown in the table.

x0123
f(x)471013

Function g is defined by g(x) = x2 + 2x − 4.

Which statement is true?
options: When x = 5, g(x) is greater than f(x).
f and g have the same y-intercept.
From x = 3 to x = 5, f increases more than g does.
g(x) is less than f(x) for every value of x greater than 0.
items.hint: Find the rule for f from the table (start value and constant change). Then substitute values into both functions.
items.explain:
From the table, f starts at 4 and goes up 3 each step, so f(x) = 3x + 4.

x = 5: f(5) = 3(5) + 4 = 19 and g(5) = 25 + 10 − 4 = 31. Since 31 > 19, g(x) is greater than f(x) when x = 5. True.

y-intercepts: f(0) = 4 and g(0) = −4. Not the same.

From x = 3 to x = 5: f goes from 13 to 19 (up 6). g(3) = 9 + 6 − 4 = 11 and g(5) = 31 (up 20). g increases more, so the statement is false.

“For every x greater than 0”: g(4) = 16 + 8 − 4 = 20 and f(4) = 16, so g is greater at x = 4. The statement is false.

This shows the key pattern: a parabola that opens up may start below a line, but it eventually passes it.
